scenes.tts: Your cortex is only about twice as thick as a mouse's. Yet its surface is roughly a thousand times larger. That is the puzzle. Across mammals, thickness changes little, while area changes enormously. How does a growing brain make more area without a thicker wall?
scenes.visual: A mouse cortex strip and a human cortex strip drawn side by side: thickness bars about 1 to 2, surface sheets about 1 to 1000 (schematic, not to scale); question marks over the wall.
scenes.narration: Your cortex is only about twice as thick as a mouse's. Yet its surface is roughly a thousand times larger. That is the puzzle. Across mammals, thickness changes little, while area changes enormously. How does a growing brain make more area without a thicker wall?

scenes.tts: Pasko Rakic studied the fetal rhesus monkey. Young neurons climb radial glial fibres. In 1988 he proposed the radial unit hypothesis. In his model, each patch of progenitors, one unit, makes one column. Related neurons can spread sideways. The number of units sets the area. The number of neurons in each unit sets the thickness.
scenes.visual: A ventricle bar with progenitor patches; neurons climb a fibre from one patch and stack into a column. Many columns side by side labelled area; one column labelled thickness.
scenes.narration: Pasko Rakic studied the fetal rhesus monkey. Young neurons climb radial glial fibres. In 1988 he proposed the radial unit hypothesis. In his model, each patch of progenitors, one unit, makes one column. Related neurons can spread sideways. The number of units sets the area. The number of neurons in each unit sets the thickness.

scenes.tts: Here is the arithmetic. While founder cells divide symmetrically, the pool doubles each round. Once they switch, each extra direct division adds only one neuron to a column. In a simple model, three more symmetric rounds give two times two times two. That is eight times as many units. Three extra asymmetric divisions add just three neurons to each column. That is small by comparison.

scenes.visual: Model panel: one unit doubles 1, 2, 4, 8 (three symmetric rounds) so the row of columns widens eightfold at the same height. Beside it a single column gains three blocks, a small rise in height.

scenes.tts: Rakic proposed that a delay of only a few cell cycles could account for a large increase in cortical area across primates. One test came from mice. Anjen Chenn and Christopher Walsh made transgenic mice whose progenitors carried a stabilized form of beta-catenin. More progenitors kept re-entering the cell cycle. Their cortex enlarged and buckled into folds, though not the way primate cortex folds.

scenes.tts: In primates, the ventricle is not the only address. In human fetal cortex, filmed in slices, outer radial glia sit far from the ventricle. They keep a long fibre to the brain surface but have no process touching the ventricle. They divide there and renew themselves. Their fibres diverge and fan the scaffold outward. These cells are abundant in primates and ferret, and rare in mouse. The marmoset has them too, yet its cortex is nearly smooth. So they do not guarantee folding.
scenes.visual: Cross-section of the wall: ventricle at the bottom with a classical radial glia attached; an outer radial glia higher up with a fibre to the surface and no ventricle contact; fibres fan out. A species strip: ferret and primate many, mouse few, marmoset has them but smooth.

scenes.tts: Three duplicated genes found in humans, not chimpanzees, have been tested. A R H G A P eleven B increased basal progenitors in mouse embryos, and enlarged the neocortex in marmoset fetuses. Notch two N L kept progenitors dividing in mouse, and deleting it made human organoid progenitors differentiate early. But none was tested by removing the gene from a developing human brain. None shows that one gene made the human cortex. Keep the idea. A longer founder phase is one route to more area.
